Full Inclusion
fool in-KLOO-zhun
noun phrase
An activist and mainline-church term naming the goal-state of affirming theology: the complete incorporation of LGBTQ persons into the life of the church — membership, marriage, ministry, and ordination — with no requirement of repentance or change. 'Full' is the operative word: anything short of unconditional incorporation is branded partial, grudging, or unjust.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

⚖️ Biblical Verdict

🔴
Reject
Incorporation with no repentance required; the gospel includes every kind of sinner precisely by calling them out of sin — 'but ye are washed.'

📖 Biblical Definition

The gospel is gloriously inclusive of sinners, but it includes them by calling them out of sin, not by leaving them in it. The same chapter that names the unrighteous who 'shall not inherit the kingdom of God' — fornicators, idolaters, adulterers, the effeminate, abusers of themselves with mankind, thieves, drunkards, revilers, extortioners — declares the gospel's true inclusion: 'And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God' (1 Cor. 6:11). Every kind of sinner is included; none is included as he is. Christ's banquet truly goes out into the highways to gather 'as many as ye shall find' (Matt. 22:9), yet the guest found without a wedding garment is cast out (Matt. 22:11-13) — the garment being the imputed righteousness of Christ received by repentance and faith. Inclusion in the kingdom is real, total, and free; it is inclusion by way of the new birth, not by way of affirmation.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The goal-state of affirming theology: no repentance required for membership or ordination; but the gospel includes all kinds of sinners precisely by calling them out of sin — 'such were some of you... but ye are washed' (1 Cor. 6:11).

FULL INCLUSION, noun phrase. The complete incorporation of LGBTQ persons into membership, marriage, and ordination with no call to repentance.

An activist/mainline term for the end-goal of affirming theology; 'full' brands any requirement of change as partial or unjust.

The gospel's inclusion: every kind of sinner washed and made new (1 Cor. 6:11); included by the new birth, not affirmed as he is.

The wedding garment (Matt. 22:11-13): the banquet gathers all, but none remains without Christ's righteousness put on by faith.

📖 Key Scripture

1 Corinthians 6:11 — "And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God."

Matthew 22:11-13 — "And when the king came in to see the guests, he saw there a man which had not on a wedding garment: And he saith unto him, Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment? And he was speechless. Then said the king to the servants, Bind him hand and foot, and take him away, and cast him into outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth."

John 3:3 — "Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God."

Acts 2:38 — "Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost."

2 Corinthians 5:17 — "Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Affirming theology's goal-state demands incorporation with no repentance; but the gospel's inclusion is inclusion by the new birth — every kind of sinner washed, sanctified, justified, never left as he was.

expand to see more

The corruption is in the word 'full,' which is made to mean 'unconditional.' Biblical inclusion is wonderfully full in one sense — it excludes no category of sinner, reaching the fornicator and the idolater and the extortioner alike — but it is inclusion on terms, and the terms are repentance and the new birth. 'Full inclusion' as a program strikes out the terms and keeps only the incorporation: come in, be a member, be married, be ordained, exactly as you are, with no call to be made new. It is precisely the man without the wedding garment, brought into the banquet hall but not clothed in the righteousness that admits him to the feast (Matt. 22:11). The king's question to that man — 'how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment?' — is the question the program cannot answer. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the 'full inclusion' goal of incorporating LGBTQ practice without repentance is named here to rebut it.

The deepest error is that 'full inclusion' makes the new birth optional. Christ told Nicodemus, 'Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God' (John 3:3) — not 'unless he is excluded by an unkind church' but 'unless he is born again.' Peter's word to the convicted crowd was 'Repent' (Acts 2:38), and Paul's description of every soul in Christ is 'a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new' (2 Cor. 5:17). A theology that includes men without this transformation has not widened the gospel; it has emptied it, offering a kingdom-membership that the King says is impossible without a birth from above. To be 'fully included' on those terms is to be brought near the feast and yet to remain in outer darkness.

The recovery is to preach the gospel's true and total inclusiveness: 'such were some of you: but ye are washed' (1 Cor. 6:11). No sinner is too far, no sin too deep; the door is open to all who will come. But all who come, come to be washed, sanctified, justified, born again — and that is not a grudging restriction on inclusion but the very substance of it, for to be included in the kingdom is to be made new. The church that calls every sinner to repentance and faith is offering the only inclusion worth having; the church that offers incorporation without the new birth is offering a counterfeit that cannot save.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The end-goal of affirming theology — incorporation without repentance; answered by the gospel's real inclusion, which washes and renews every kind of sinner (1 Cor. 6:11) and admits none without the wedding garment of Christ's righteousness.

expand to see more

English: an activist/mainline term for the goal-state of affirming theology; 'full' brands any call to change as unjust.

The gospel's inclusion: 1 Cor. 6:11 — 'such were some of you: but ye are washed' — all kinds of sinners, none left as he was.

The condition: John 3:3 and Acts 2:38 — the new birth and repentance; inclusion in the kingdom is by transformation, not affirmation.

Usage

"'Full inclusion' keeps the banquet and strikes out the wedding garment — but the king still asks how a man came in without it."

"Christ did not say 'except a man be welcomed warmly'; He said 'except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.'"

"The gospel excludes no kind of sinner and includes none as he is; it washes, sanctifies, justifies — that is the only inclusion that saves."
